classification_signals: The article describes the author's 'own experiment with creating audio trails' (p. 12).
It states, 'I surveyed over 150 people who tried the memoryscape audio trails. People responded extremely positively...' (p. 15), indicating primary data collection.
The findings are qualitative themes and direct quotes from participants, characteristic of qualitative research.
The paper also includes an extensive narrative review of sound art and oral history practices (p. 3-12).
title: Memoryscape: how audio walks can deepen our sense of place by integrating art, oral history and cultural geography

limitations: The findings are based on qualitative self-report data from a survey, without statistical analysis or control groups.
The study is a case study of the author's own 'practice-based research', which may introduce researcher bias.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper explores how audio walks, or 'memoryscapes,' can deepen a sense of place by integrating sound art, oral history, and cultural geography. It reviews the historical development of sound walks from artistic and oral history practices, highlighting examples like John Cage and Janet Cardiff. The author then presents findings from their own practice-based research, where over 150 participants experienced memoryscape audio trails along the River Thames. Qualitative feedback indicated that hearing authentic local voices and stories connected to the landscape fostered feelings of closeness, rootedness, and empathy, enhancing their understanding and attachment to the place. The physical act of walking combined with located sound and memory created a multi-layered experience, allowing participants to imagine past events and remember stories when revisiting the sites.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Abstract
                  This article is concerned with the history and practice of creating sound walks or ‘memoryscapes’: outdoor trails that use recorded sound and spoken memory played on a personal stereo or mobile media to experience places in new ways. In this relatively new and rapidly evolving field, the author brings together works from music, sound art, oral history and cultural geography as a starting point to understanding how such trails can give us a more sophisticated and nuanced experience of places. He suggests that this might offer some exciting opportunities for practice‐based multimedia research and teaching.
